headline: US markets surged last night on Iran ceasefire hopes and strong tech earnings, lifting the ASX 1.1% today — but Take-Two Interactive dropped 3.5% on a cautious GTA 6 outlook that rattled investors.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft had a strong night on NASDAQ, rising 2.75% to $545.18. No specific news catalyst, but the broader tech rally driven by easing geopolitical fears (US-Iran tensions cooling) and AI optimism lifted the whole sector. MSFT is now up 23% on your cost base — a solid long-term performer.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two fell 3.48% last night after the company gave a 'restrained' near-term financial outlook ahead of the GTA 6 launch next week. CEO Strauss Zelnick said pre-sales are 'far in excess' of expectations and promised the game won't be delayed again, but investors got spooked by cautious guidance. This is a classic pre-launch jitter — the actual release could be the catalyst that turns sentiment around.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI bounced 2.23% today, riding the global AI tailwind and a strong ASX session. The fund tracks AI-focused companies, so the broader tech rally overnight in the US flowed through. Still down 17.5% on your cost base, but today's move is a step in the right direction.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG had a solid session, up 2.0% as both the ASX and global markets rallied. As a diversified high-growth ETF with heavy US exposure, it benefits directly from strong nights on Wall Street and calmer geopolitical conditions. Essentially flat on your overall cost base now.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS climbed 1.61% today, reflecting the strong S&P 500 and NASDAQ session from last night. This ETF mirrors the entire US sharemarket, so a 2.35% S&P rally flows straight through. Up 4% on your cost base — the long-term US market story remains intact.

movers.name: DHHF (BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF)
movers.note: DHHF gained 1.49% in today's session, buoyed by the broad ASX rally and positive global sentiment. A well-diversified all-growth fund that moves with world markets — nothing dramatic here, just a good day.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google edged up 0.73% last night but underperformed the broader NASDAQ (+2.74%). JPMorgan removed Alphabet from its Analyst Focus List, which likely weighed on sentiment relative to peers. The long-term story — Search dominance, YouTube, cloud, AI — hasn't changed. Still slightly down on your cost base overall.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara nudged up 0.69% today in a broadly positive ASX session. The lithium sector remains under pressure — Scotiabank this week cut its price target on major lithium producer Albemarle citing a weaker lithium price outlook, which is the same headwind hitting PLS. Still deeply underwater at -57% on your cost base.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE barely moved today, up just 0.23%. Emerging markets tend to lag when the US dollar is stronger, and geopolitical tensions (Iran conflict, Middle East instability) make investors more cautious about developing economies. Down 4.7% on your cost base — a slow grind but no structural change.

watch_today.title: Take-Two (TTWO): Hold through GTA 6 launch jitters
watch_today.detail: TTWO dropped 3.48% last night after cautious near-term guidance, but CEO Strauss Zelnick confirmed pre-sales are 'far in excess' of expectations and the game launches next week. For a long-term holder, this pre-launch volatility is noise — if GTA 6 delivers commercially (and all signs point to yes), the stock has a real catalyst ahead. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: Microsoft (MSFT): Strong session, long-term story intact
watch_today.detail: MSFT surged 2.75% last night to $545.18, now up 23% on your cost base. No single news catalyst — just AI and tech optimism plus easing Iran tensions lifting the whole sector. Nothing to do here except enjoy it. Hold.

watch_today.title: Pilbara Minerals (PLS): Lithium outlook still challenged
watch_today.detail: PLS ticked up 0.69% today but remains down 57% on your cost base. Scotiabank this week cut its price target on Albemarle (a global lithium bellwether) citing a lower lithium price outlook — the same pressure weighing on PLS. No sign of a structural turnaround yet. Unless your thesis has changed, hold and wait for lithium demand to recover.

watch_today.title: GXAI: AI tailwind building — consider topping up on dips
watch_today.detail: GXAI rose 2.23% today and the broader AI story is accelerating — Anthropic just launched models beating Google and OpenAI on key benchmarks, and the Australian government announced a new AI regulator, signalling the sector is maturing. GXAI is still down 17.5% on your cost base, but for a long-term buyer the AI structural story is very much alive. Worth watching for further dips as a top-up opportunity.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike impact on your portfolio
watch_today.detail: The RBA raised rates again in November (confirmed by savings rate articles today), and the central bank has warned that Australia's AI data centre building boom is keeping inflation elevated — meaning rates could stay higher for longer. This is a headwind for growth stocks and ETFs broadly, but your diversified holdings (VDHG, DHHF, VTS) are built to weather rate cycles over the long run.

watch_today.title: GTA 6 launches next week — TTWO in focus
watch_today.detail: Take-Two's CEO confirmed GTA 6 goes on sale next week and pre-sales are tracking 'far in excess' of expectations. This is the most significant product launch in gaming history by some measures. Watch the launch week sales data closely — a strong opening could quickly reverse last night's sell-off.

world.summary: The big story today is the apparent end of the US-Iran conflict, with Trump declaring the war 'effectively over' militarily after meeting with Gulf leaders. Meanwhile, Stephen Miller takes over as White House chief of staff, Ukraine struck a major Russian oil refinery, and Russia's last major independent newspaper shut its doors under government pressure.

stories.title: Trump declares US-Iran war 'effectively over' after Gulf leader talks
stories.why_it_matters: President Trump met with Qatar's Prime Minister and declared the US-Iran military conflict 'effectively over', saying further US attacks on Iran are 'highly unlikely'. Trump said Qatar and Saudi Arabia both prefer peace. This is a massive de-escalation — oil prices dipped 1.4% to $85.61/barrel partly on these signals, and global sharemarkets rallied hard last night. If the ceasefire holds, it removes a major risk premium from global markets that had been building for months.

stories.title: Stephen Miller becomes White House chief of staff
stories.why_it_matters: Hardline immigration and policy aide Stephen Miller has taken over as White House chief of staff, one of the most powerful jobs in the US government. Miller is the architect of Trump's most aggressive immigration policies and has long pushed for maximum executive power. His elevation signals Trump's second term is about to get significantly more assertive on domestic and foreign policy — this will have ripple effects on trade, immigration, and international relations that matter to Australian exporters and investors.

stories.title: Ukraine strikes Russia's second-largest oil refinery
stories.why_it_matters: Ukraine launched a major strike on Russia's second-largest oil refinery (a Rosneft facility), causing significant damage that forced Rosneft to cap fuel sales. This is one of Ukraine's most significant energy infrastructure attacks to date — it directly hits Russia's ability to fund its war machine through oil revenues. For everyday Australians, disruptions to Russian energy supply can push up global oil prices, though the Iran ceasefire news is currently pulling in the opposite direction.

stories.title: Russia's top independent newspaper shuts after three decades under government pressure
stories.why_it_matters: Russia's most prominent independent newspaper has closed its Moscow office after more than 30 years of operation, citing sustained official pressure from the Kremlin. This is another significant blow to press freedom in Russia — the paper had long been one of the few outlets reporting critically on the government. With independent media now effectively silenced, Russians have even fewer windows to alternative information about the war in Ukraine and domestic affairs.

stories.title: Trump questions midterm election results, raising democratic stability concerns
stories.why_it_matters: Trump has reverted to claiming the recent US midterm elections were rigged, setting up a bitter confrontation with Congress. This mirrors the playbook from 2020 and signals major political turbulence ahead in Washington. A gridlocked or contested Congress could stall legislation on trade, the debt ceiling, and foreign aid — all of which have knock-on effects for global markets and Australia's major trading relationships.

markets.summary: A very strong night on Wall Street last night, with the S&P 500 up 2.35% and the NASDAQ up 2.74% — driven largely by US-Iran ceasefire signals and broad tech strength. The ASX followed suit today, closing up 1.1% at 9,129. The Aussie dollar rose to US69.25 cents. Oil fell 1.4% on the geopolitical de-escalation, while gold edged up slightly to $4,128/oz.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Solid session today, lifted by last night's Wall Street rally and Iran ceasefire news.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Big night last night — Iran de-escalation and tech strength drove the broad US market up 2.35%.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech roared last night, up 2.74%, with Microsoft leading the charge.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil fell 1.4% as Trump's declaration that the Iran conflict is 'effectively over' eased supply-disruption fears.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold nudged up slightly — still near record highs as investors keep some defensive positioning despite the geopolitical calm.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar rose to US69.25 cents — a stronger risk appetite globally tends to push the AUD up.

politics.summary: The Albanese government had a big day on AI regulation, announcing a new national AI regulator and mandatory reporting rules after a major OpenAI security breach exposed Medicare data. Meanwhile, there's growing internal Labor tension over Treasurer Jim Chalmers, with colleagues publicly calling for the leaks against him to stop. The RBA's rate hike is also generating debate about who actually benefits.

stories.title: Albanese announces new AI regulator and mandatory security reporting laws
stories.why_it_matters: PM Albanese announced a new national AI regulator today, alongside laws requiring AI companies to mandatorily report security incidents to the government. The move comes directly after OpenAI suffered a breach that exposed Medicare data — a stark reminder that AI systems now hold sensitive personal information about millions of Australians. Companies that fail to report incidents could face criminal penalties under proposed law changes. This is a significant step toward Australia having a formal AI governance framework.

stories.title: Internal Labor leaks against Jim Chalmers sparking cabinet tension
stories.why_it_matters: Multiple Labor ministers have gone public demanding the internal leaking against Treasurer Jim Chalmers stops immediately. Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek was among those urging colleagues to 'stop undermining' Chalmers. Reports suggest Treasury has effectively been 'silenced' and left out of the loop on some tax policy proposals. The infighting signals serious cracks in Labor's economic team at a critical time — just as the government is trying to manage inflation, rate hikes, and a contested budget.

stories.title: RBA rate hike: who actually benefits?
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA's November rate hike has savings account rates ticking up across major banks. SMH points out today that most Australians don't actually have a mortgage — meaning the majority of people are net beneficiaries of higher interest rates through better returns on savings and term deposits. The debate highlights that the standard 'rate rises hurt everyone' narrative is more nuanced than it sounds, particularly for retirees and savers on the Gold Coast.

stories.title: RBA warns AI data centre boom is keeping rates higher for longer
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has warned in a new speech that the massive AI data centre construction boom sweeping Australia is contributing to inflation — driving up energy demand, construction costs, and skilled labour wages. The RBA says this structural cost pressure means interest rates may need to stay elevated for longer than previously expected. For mortgage holders and investors, this is a signal that rate relief is not imminent.

ai.summary: Big AI news today: Australia is getting a formal AI regulator after the OpenAI-Medicare data breach, Anthropic's new AI models are beating Google and OpenAI on benchmarks, and the RBA is warning that the AI infrastructure boom is an inflationary force in its own right.

stories.title: OpenAI suffered a Medicare data breach — now Australia is mandating AI incident reporting
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI suffered a security breach that exposed Medicare data belonging to Australians — a significant hack of a system that holds sensitive health records. In response, the Albanese government today announced laws requiring all AI companies operating in Australia to report security incidents to regulators, or face criminal penalties. This is a direct and consequential response to a real-world AI failure — your personal health data is now on the agenda of AI regulators.

stories.title: Anthropic's new Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 models beat Google and OpenAI on most benchmarks
stories.why_it_matters: Anthropic (the AI safety company backed by Google and Amazon) has launched two new models — Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 — that outperform both Google's Gemini 4 Carbon and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on the majority of standard AI performance benchmarks. In plain English: a third major player is now genuinely ahead on raw capability tests. This intensifies the AI arms race and is a tailwind for your GXAI.AX holding, which invests broadly across AI companies.

stories.title: Australia announces new AI regulator with 'significant penalties' for non-compliance
stories.why_it_matters: Beyond just incident reporting, the Australian government today unveiled a broader mandatory AI compliance framework overseen by a new national regulator. PM Albanese promised 'significant penalties' for companies that breach the guardrails. The regulator will have powers to investigate 'frontier' AI companies (the most advanced systems) and the government is also considering criminal law changes to hold erring companies to account. Australia is one of the first countries to move from voluntary AI guidelines to mandatory enforceable rules.

stories.title: RBA: AI is making workers more productive — but also making your cost of living higher right now
stories.why_it_matters: In a major speech, the RBA laid out its view on AI and the economy: long term, AI will likely boost worker productivity and potentially lower prices. But right now, the AI construction boom — data centres, power infrastructure, specialised labour — is adding to inflationary pressure. The RBA said 'intelligence is getting cheaper' (meaning AI tools cost less each year) but the physical infrastructure needed to run AI is driving up energy and construction costs across Australia today.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — the Roosters edged the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. Post-match, the controversies are flying: ref complaints, a player facing a ban for a ref gesture, and a Broncos star copping a drink-driving suspension. Plus, a 13-year-old Gold Coast surfing prodigy is making waves nationally.

stories.title: Roosters win the 2026 NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Knights
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters claimed the 2026 NRL premiership with a heart-stopping 19-18 victory over the Newcastle Knights at Accor Stadium on Sunday evening. One point separated the two sides at the final whistle — it doesn't get closer than that. The Knights' heartbreak was compounded by post-match controversy, with Panthers great and commentator Jarome Luai calling out the referee and the Knights' skipper reportedly storming off. A game that will be talked about for years.

stories.title: Star Eels recruit facing ban over ref gesture at World Cup
stories.why_it_matters: A newly signed Parramatta Eels recruit is facing a potential NRL ban after making a controversial gesture directed at a referee during the Rugby League World Cup. The NRL is investigating the incident and a suspension is expected to be handed down shortly. The timing is awful for the Eels — they signed this player as a marquee recruit and may start next season short-handed.

stories.title: Broncos star handed drink-driving ban by NRL
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL has handed a Brisbane Broncos player a formal ban for a drink-driving offence. The duration of the suspension has been confirmed but wasn't specified in reports — the Broncos' off-season is now complicated heading into pre-season preparation. It's another off-field discipline issue for a club that has been trying to rebuild its culture.

stories.title: Gold Coast's 13-year-old surfing prodigy Leihani Zoric: 'I don't want to participate, I want to dominate'
stories.why_it_matters: Local news for Gold Coasters — 13-year-old Leihani Zoric is being described as one of Australia's most exciting young surfing talents, and The Guardian has run a major profile on her today. The young Gold Coast prodigy is already making waves nationally and internationally, with coaches and former champions tipping her for a World Surf League future. Worth keeping an eye on — this kid sounds like the real deal.

stories.title: Rugby League World Cup 2030 adopts travelling Magic Round format
stories.why_it_matters: The 2030 Rugby League World Cup has confirmed it will adopt a travelling Magic Round format, rotating the event's showcase rounds across multiple host cities rather than fixing them in one venue. This is a significant structural change that could mean more World Cup action coming to Queensland — including potentially the Gold Coast. The format is designed to maximise crowds and commercial revenue across the tournament.
